And you'll be further down from the monad. So this is how intuitively we've understood the universe to work: when we're born, we're almost with an intuitive understanding of this. The problem is that as our populations continue to grow and grow, eventually we have war. And war gives rise to patriarchy and property. Why? Because how do you incentivize people to go fight? Well, you promise them a wife will be yours; you'll be the master of the household and whatever you win—whether it's gold or whatever—it will be yours forever. And so these three things: war, patriarchy, and property are all interlinked together. This you can argue gives rise to the idea of capital.

Remember when we last discussed the bronze age; the bronze age was the height of capital and therefore it was the height of war, slavery, corruption, violence, evil in this world. And in this time there will emerge prophets—port prophets—who come and tell us that what we're doing is wrong. We must remember who we came from originally: we are part of the monad and that we're here to celebrate life, not to destroy it; to be creative, not destructive; to love, not to make war.

During the bronze age emerges a man named Zoroaster (Zorathustra) and he is a port prophet just like Homer and Yahweh. He's dealing with a situation where war, patriarchal rule, and property are prevalent and we can't imagine a world without these things. So now he has to create a new system. He presents poetry with new ideas that help us return to the monad. And so he creates the beginnings of a new world religion called Zorastrianism (Zurashinism). So let's go over the basic ideas: remember this is a polytheistic world where you fight for your god. The gods don't really care about what's good and what's evil; all they care about is themselves. You celebrate them, make sacrifices to them. If you give them enough money or bought them well enough, then you win wars.

Azaraster (Aurora Master) reimagines the system and creates a new hierarchy where Ahura Mazda is the top god, also known as the monad. For Zoroaster, Ahura Mazda is the lord of wisdom, literally translated into "lord of wisdom" and he's represented by the idea of fire.

In Chinese, astorism (Zorastrianism) is called 白火教 (bái huǒ jiào), a religion of wisdom. And what Zoroaster also says is that the war of heaven and hell is within us. There are two forces that tear at us and divide us: the force of asha, which means truth, and dusham, which means lie. The Greeks really admired the Persians for their honesty; they said the Persians are good at three things: horse riding, archery, and telling the truth.

Telling the truth is not what asha is; it's a system of virtue. By being virtuous by doing good in the world, you become closer to Ahura Mazda, his representative on earth. To better understand this idea, let me introduce another concept called the categorical imperative. Emanuel Kant lived about 3,000 years after Zoroaster (we don't know when he lived but about 3,000 years ago), and he introduced a concept called the categorical imperative.

For Kant, the categorical imperative is the highest moral law, what we all should strive for. What I will show you is that it's very similar to the concept of asha. The first principle of the categorical imperative is the law of universality. This idea states that what is good? Well, imagine this: whatever you do or say, everyone in the world would immediately do as well.
